content.text:
The telephone arrived in a crowded field. Alexander Graham Bell, a teacher of the deaf who had studied how sound could be made visible, was working on a multiple telegraph that could send several messages down one wire at once. In the process he became convinced that the human voice itself could be transmitted electrically. On March 7, 1876, the United States Patent Office granted him patent number 174,465 for "improvement in telegraphy." The same day, the rival inventor Elisha Gray filed a notice of an invention, called a caveat, describing a similar device that used a liquid transmitter. Whether Gray's filing was a direct challenge or a coincidence has been argued over ever since, and later litigation over the patent reached the Supreme Court more than once.

Three days after the patent was granted, on March 10, 1876, Bell spoke into his instrument in his Boston laboratory. The words he used, addressed to his assistant Thomas Watson in the next room, were "Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you." Watson heard them through a receiver in the other room. The device was crude, and the sound was faint and distorted, but it worked, and it demonstrated that speech could travel along a wire in a form that a listener could understand.

The early years were a matter of refinement and promotion. Bell and his backers, including his father-in-law Gardiner Greene Hubbard, formed the Bell Telephone Company in 1877. Bell himself showed the instrument at the Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia in 1876, where Emperor Dom Pedro II of Brazil reportedly reacted with surprise, and the device drew wide public curiosity. The first telephones were sold or leased in pairs, so that two subscribers could talk only to each other. Each line was a private connection, and there was no way to call an arbitrary third party. A network of many subscribers required a different arrangement entirely.

That arrangement was the switchboard. Early exchanges were installed in cities in the late 1870s and 1880s, and a subscriber who wanted to reach someone else would ring a central office, where an operator connected a cord between the two lines. The operators were largely young women, who were hired because companies believed they were patient and courteous, and who were expected to be polite, quick and discreet. Their work defined the early telephone's social character. Callers spoke to a human intermediary before they reached anyone else, and the job carried strict rules about conduct and appearance.

The switchboard had problems of its own. Mistakes were common, and some operators were accused of listening in or of favoring certain customers. Almon Brown Strowger, an undertaker in Kansas City, reportedly believed that a local telephone operator was diverting calls meant for his business to a competitor. In response he patented an automatic exchange in 1891, in which the caller's dial pulses drove electromechanical switches that connected the line without a human operator. Automatic exchanges spread slowly at first, since they were expensive and the Bell system was reluctant to change its methods, but they gradually became the standard, and the dial telephone eventually became common in homes across the world.

Distance was the next great obstacle. A signal sent over a long wire loses strength, and the wire's electrical properties blur high-frequency sounds, so voices at long range were muffled and hard to understand. Engineers attacked the problem with better wire and with loading coils, inductors spaced along the line to restore clarity. Michael Pupin and George Ashley Campbell developed the theory and practice of loading in the first decade of the twentieth century, and it made much longer lines practical. In 1915, a line between New York and San Francisco was completed, and Bell and Watson repeated their famous conversation for the occasion, with Bell in New York and Watson in San Francisco.

Crossing the ocean was harder still. The first transatlantic telephone service, a radio link, opened in 1927 and was expensive and unreliable, prone to fading and static. Submarine telephone cables became feasible only after the development of vacuum-tube amplifiers and then coaxial cable. The first transatlantic telephone cable, TAT-1, opened in 1956, carrying a limited number of simultaneous calls. Later cables, satellites and eventually fiber-optic lines multiplied capacity many times over.

Over the twentieth century the telephone changed from a luxury into a household necessity, and it reshaped social habits. It made businesses faster and more responsive, gave families a way to keep in touch across distances, and created new kinds of work, from operators to telephone engineers. It also raised concerns about privacy and about the power of a single regulated monopoly. In the United States the Bell System was for decades the dominant provider of service and equipment, and its dominance was finally broken up by a 1982 antitrust settlement that took effect in 1984, separating long-distance service from local operating companies.

The telephone's later history is largely one of convergence. Mobile telephony, first deployed in limited form in the 1940s and 1950s and made practical by cellular networks in the 1980s, removed the wire from the handset. Digital switching, data networks and the internet then absorbed voice into a broader stream of packets, so that a call today is usually just another form of data. Yet the basic arrangement that Bell demonstrated in 1876 remains: a sound is turned into an electrical pattern, carried across distance, and turned back into sound at the other end.
